transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Um... well, I guess I’m here because... I just feel like I really don’t deserve the trust people put in me. I keep replaying these small clinical imperfections in my head, over and over, as if they prove I’m a dangerous doctor. 

It's just exhausting. Actually, speaking of being a doctor, parking around this clinic is pretty intense, isn't it? I had to park three blocks down by that little bakery. I used to go to a bakery just like that when I was getting my associate's degree before I went on to med school. They had these amazing blueberry scones. I tried baking scones once a couple of years ago, but I completely burned the bottoms of them because my oven thermostat was broken. I ended up having to buy a whole new heating element online and install it myself. Took me like three hours and a bunch of YouTube tutorials to figure it out. 

But, um... yeah, anyway, I just keep obsessing over every little mistake I make at work.
Do you ever have thoughts that feel intrusive or unwanted that you try to push away or neutralize by doing something else in your mind or through certain actions?

Um, intrusive thoughts... like pushing them away? I don't think so. I mean, I just obsess over the mistakes, but I don't really do any actions or anything to neutralize them. I just sit there and feel terrible. Actually, speaking of sitting there, I spend a lot of time sitting in my office chair. It's one of those ergonomic ones, you know? The mesh kind. I bought it on sale last Black Friday. I was originally looking for a new monitor because mine had this weird dead pixel right in the middle of the screen. It was so annoying, especially when I was reviewing charts. I tried all those pixel-fixing videos on YouTube where they flash different colors really fast, but it didn't work. So I went to the electronics store, and they didn't have the monitor I wanted, but they had a huge sale on office chairs. 

So, yeah... I don't really do anything to neutralize the thoughts. They just kind of stay there.
Have you ever felt driven to perform certain routines, behaviors, or mental acts over and over again in response to these obsessive thoughts, even if you don’t really want to?

No, I don't really do anything over and over. I mean, the thoughts just kind of loop, but I don't have any routines or behaviors like that. I just feel guilty. Like I'm a fraud. 

But routines... you know, the only routine I really have is my morning coffee. I have to use this specific French press I got when I was in undergrad. It's got a little crack on the glass, but it still works perfectly. I actually tried switching to a drip machine a few months ago because my mornings were getting so rushed. I found one at a thrift store near my apartment. The thrift store is right next to this dry cleaner I used to use, but they ruined one of my favorite dress shirts. They completely melted the collar somehow. I tried to get them to pay for it, but the owner just pointed to this tiny sign on the wall that said they aren't responsible for damage. I was so mad I just walked out. 

But anyway, no, I don't do any repetitive acts or anything like that. Just the thoughts.
Do you ever feel a strong need to do something repeatedly, like checking things, counting, or following strict routines, even if you don’t really want to?

I feel like you just asked me that... but no, I don't. I don't count things or check the stove a hundred times or anything. I just sit with the guilt. 

Speaking of stoves, though, my landlord just replaced mine last week. The old one was gas, and the pilot light kept going out. It smelled like gas in the kitchen half the time, which is probably super dangerous. I had to call him like four times before he finally sent someone out. The guy who came to install the new one was actually a patient of mine a couple of years ago. He had this nasty laceration on his arm from a piece of sheet metal. I stitched him up, and I remember thinking at the time that I probably didn't use the right gauge suture, even though it healed fine. Seeing him again just brought all that back up, you know? Like, what if I had messed up his arm permanently? 

But yeah, to answer your question, no checking or counting routines. Just the thoughts.
Do you ever feel like you have to repeat certain thoughts or behaviors, like checking, washing, or counting, even if you don't really want to?

Doctor, I... I'm pretty sure we just went over this. Like I said, no. I don't wash my hands a million times or count things. I don't do any of that stuff. 

Washing, though... I really need to do laundry. My washing machine has been making this awful thumping noise during the spin cycle. It sounds like someone is in there with a hammer. I tried to level the feet on it, because I read online that an unbalanced machine can cause that, but it didn't help. I even bought this special wrench for it, but the space in my laundry closet is so tight I kept scraping my knuckles on the wall. The wall in there is painted this awful mustard yellow color. I've been meaning to repaint it since I moved in, but I just... I don't have the energy for it. I bought the paint, though. It's sitting in the trunk of my car. It's a nice, calming gray. I thought gray would be better. 

But no, I don't have any behaviors or routines I have to repeat. I just feel bad about everything.
Do you ever find yourself mentally trying to undo or neutralize distressing thoughts with other thoughts, prayers, or mental rituals, even if you don’t act them out physically?

No, I don't really do anything like that. I don't try to cancel the thoughts out with prayers or other thoughts. They just sit there, and I just feel... terrible. Like I should be punished, you know? 

Speaking of prayers, though, my grandmother used to pray all the time. She had this rosary she brought over from Italy, and the beads were made of olive wood. She told me once that the wood came from a tree near where she grew up. I actually visited Italy a few years ago, right after I finished my residency. I went to Florence, and the food there was just incredible. I had this wild boar ragu that I still think about sometimes. I tried to recreate it at home, but I couldn't find the right kind of pasta. I went to three different grocery stores looking for pappardelle, but they only had fettuccine. It just wasn't the same. The sauce didn't cling to it right. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't do any mental rituals or try to undo the thoughts. They just stay with me.

Have you ever felt the need to do something repeatedly, even if it’s not in response to a troubling thought, like needing to arrange objects a certain way, repeat actions a specific number of times, or follow a precise routine to feel 'just right'?

Doctor, I... didn't we just talk about this? Or something really similar? No, I don't arrange things or do things a certain number of times to feel right. Nothing like that. 

Arranging things... you know, I tried to organize my desk at the clinic last week. It was getting completely out of hand, just piles of charts and drug rep pamphlets everywhere. I bought these little acrylic organizers, thinking they would help. But they were too small for the standard folders we use, so they just ended up taking up more space. I ended up giving them to one of the medical assistants. She used them for her makeup, I think. She's always wearing this really bright blue eyeliner. It's a very specific shade, almost like a cobalt blue. I asked her once where she got it, because my sister was looking for something similar for a Halloween costume, but I can't remember what brand she said. It was some indie brand online, I think. 

But yeah, no, I don't have any routines or arranging habits I have to do. Just the guilt. Always the guilt.
Have you ever felt driven to perform certain mental acts or behaviors that you felt you had to do, even if they were time-consuming or caused you distress?

Doctor, I... I feel like we're going in circles here. I really do. Like I've been saying, no. I don't have any behaviors or mental acts I feel driven to do. Nothing time-consuming like that. 

Time-consuming... you know what's really time-consuming? Commuting. My drive to the clinic takes almost forty-five minutes on a good day. And that's if I leave before 6:30 AM. If I hit the road any later, it's easily over an hour. The traffic on I-95 is just a nightmare. They've been doing construction on the northbound side for what feels like three years now. They keep moving the concrete barriers around, so the lanes shift slightly every few weeks, and people just don't know how to handle it. Last Tuesday, there was this massive pileup because someone slammed on their brakes where the shoulder narrows. I sat parked on the highway for an hour and a half. I ended up listening to an entire podcast episode about the history of the postal service. It was actually fascinating. Did you know they used to send live animals through the mail? Like, actual children, too, for a brief period before they changed the regulations. Imagine just stamping a kid and putting them on a train. 

But anyway, no. I don't do any mental acts or behaviors that I feel forced to do. I just... I just have these awful thoughts that I deserve all the bad things happening to me. That's all.

Do you ever feel compelled to do something—like seeking reassurance, avoiding certain situations, or mentally reviewing events—to try to ease the distress from these thoughts, even if just temporarily?

Doctor, again... no. I don't. I don't seek reassurance or try to ease the distress. I don't avoid things to make the thoughts go away. I just... I just let them be there, because I feel like I deserve them. 

Seeking reassurance... you know, my dog, Buster, he's a golden retriever mix, he's always seeking reassurance. Especially during thunderstorms. If he even hears a rumble in the distance, he comes and shoves his wet nose right under my hand, demanding to be pet. He's terrified of loud noises. We tried those thundershirts, you know, the ones that are supposed to swaddle them and make them feel safe? It didn't work at all. He just looked at me like I had betrayed him, standing there in this tight little gray vest. It was actually kind of pathetic. We ended up having to get a prescription from the vet for trazodone just to get him through the Fourth of July last year. My neighbors set off fireworks for three days straight. Not even the professional ones, just those loud, obnoxious bottle rockets that sound like gunshots. I don't understand the appeal, honestly. 

But no, I don't do any of those things you're asking about. I don't try to make the thoughts stop. I just feel guilty.

Do you ever feel the need to do something — like checking, repeating actions, or thinking certain thoughts — to reduce the anxiety or guilt you feel about your mistakes, even if just for a little while?

Doctor, I... we just covered this, didn't we? I feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again. No, I don't check things or repeat actions to reduce the guilt. I don't try to reduce it at all. 

Checking things... it reminds me of when I was doing my residency. We had this one attending who was absolutely obsessed with checking lab values. Like, to a pathological degree. He would make us pull up the electronic medical record and refresh the page every five minutes if we were waiting on a stat potassium level or something. It was exhausting. And the system we used, Epic, it had this weird glitch on the monitors in the resident workroom where if you refreshed too many times in a row, the screen would just freeze and you'd have to completely restart the computer. Which, of course, took at least ten minutes because the hospital IT department insisted on running all these security protocols during startup. I remember one time, I was trying to restart the computer while eating a slightly stale blueberry muffin from the cafeteria, and I dropped half of it right on the keyboard. Getting those crumbs out from between the keys was impossible. I think that keyboard still has a sticky 'H' key to this day. 

But anyway, no. I don't do anything to try and fix the guilt. I just live with it.
